title: BTR Spectre-v2 Attack Leaks Linux Kernel Memory and Steals Root Password Hashes
content_md: A newly disclosed Branch Target Reuse (BTR) attack technique abuses stale indirect-branch predictions in just-in-time (JIT) code to leak sensitive data from Linux kernel memory. An end-to-end proof of concept demonstrated recovery of a root password hash from the memory of the su process on modern Intel systems, despite enabled mitigations. BTR targets a gap between the processor’s architectural view of code and the prediction state held in its Branch Target Buffer (BTB) . Modern processors correctly restore code coherence after code is modified, freed, or replaced. New BTR Spectre-v2 Attack Leaks Linux Kernel Memory However, they may retain stale BTB entries that point to an older indirect-branch destination. When JIT memory is recycled, an attacker can arrange for new code to occupy part of the old region, then induce the CPU to speculatively execute from the stale target. The result is effectively a speculative execute-after-free primitive. The processor transiently follows an obsolete prediction into newly generated attacker-influenced code, where a disclosure gadget can expose secret-dependent data through microarchitectural side channels. overview of the attack (Source: vusec) Architectural execution is ultimately corrected, but cache-state traces created during speculation can be measured to reconstruct the leaked value.
